records.our_prose: Violas, pansies, and Johnny-jump-ups are cheerful flowers for cool weather. Unlike most flowers, they love the cold: they keep blooming through fall, winter, and early spring in mild areas and bounce back from frost and light snow. What they cannot take is heat. Once summer warmth arrives, they get leggy, pale, and stop flowering well, so in hot areas they are grown as a fall-to-spring flower and replaced when it heats up. The flowers are edible and pretty on a salad or cake, and the little Johnny-jump-up type reseeds itself and pops up on its own year after year.

records.our_prose: Viola is the classic cool-season bedding flower: garden pansies (Viola x wittrockiana), violas or horned violets (Viola cornuta), and Johnny-jump-ups (Viola tricolor) are short-lived perennials almost always grown as cool-season annuals. They are very frost-hardy, blooming any time the temperature is above freezing and shrugging off light snow, which makes them the workhorse of fall, winter, and early-spring color in mild zones and the first and last color of the season in cold ones. Their one hard limit is heat: blooms fade, stems stretch, and plants turn ragged once sustained warmth above roughly 75 °F arrives, so in most regions they pause or are pulled through summer and return in fall. The flowers are edible, and Johnny-jump-ups self-seed and naturalize.

records.our_prose: Viola is happiest in a slightly acidic soil of about 5.4 to 5.8 and tolerates a bit either side of that. High pH is the real risk: alkaline soil triggers iron deficiency and favors black root rot, so do not lime a viola bed and correct genuinely alkaline ground before planting.
records.source_context: Placing mulch around the base can help conserve moisture and insulate the roots during cold snaps. Pansies prefer a soil pH of 5.4 to 5.8 and benefit from fertilizer application during the growing season. For home gardening, purchasing seeds, seedlings, or mature plants from reputable sources is often more effective than trying to produce your own seed stock.

records.source_context: In the spring, there should be enough rain to provide adequate moisture for pansies (about an inch of water once a week). Never water pansies in the late afternoon or evening since this encourages disease. Mix a granular slow-release fertilizer into the soil as you are planting the pansies.

records.our_prose: Violas have shallow roots and dislike both drought and waterlogging, so keep even moisture, about an inch a week whenever less than that falls as rain, letting the surface dry slightly between waterings. Water at the base in the MORNING only: never water in the late afternoon or evening, which leaves foliage and crowns wet overnight and drives viola's chief weakness, crown and root rot.
